extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics and mathematicians interested in foundations and axiomatization of geometry (graduate students, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of Hilbert's 'purity of method' investigations in the Grundlagen and related lectures: which axioms/continuity assumptions are necessary to prove elementary geometric theorems and how intuitive/spatial arguments relate to axiomatic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planar Desargues's Theorem (as sufficient condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Planar Desargues’s Theorem is a sufficient condition for the orderly incidence of lines and planes, in the sense that it can be used to generate a space; it appears to have spatial content and cannot be proved from planar axioms alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s statement and construction show the theorem has spatial content and can be taken as an axiom in place of spatial incidence axioms; modern treatments use it as an alternative axiom (e.g. in affine plane treatments). The point is that a theorem can serve as an axiom when it encodes extra (spatial) incidence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether a proof or theorem depends essentially on spatial/physical intuition (superposition, flipping, turning) or can be achieved purely from axioms without such empirical/spatial assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s investigations recast intuitive ‘purity’ questions as logical/axiomatic questions: e.g., is 'flipping' essential to the proof of ITT? This becomes: is the full Triangle Congruence Axiom a logical consequence of a restricted orientation-preserving version? Use such purity questions to probe which axioms are necessary or superfluous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isoceles Triangle Theorem (ITT) as axiomatic test
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITT (base angles equal in an isoceles triangle, equivalently equal base angles imply equal opposite sides) is used as a benchmark proposition for evaluating the strength of congruence and continuity axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Euclid’s, Pappus’s, and Hilbert’s proofs: Euclid uses superposition; Hilbert proves ITT from incidence, order, and congruence axioms (with Triangle Congruence Axiom). Use provability (or independence) of ITT to assess whether particular axioms (full/restricted congruence, Archimedean, Nachbarschaft/Einlagerung) are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle Congruence Axiom — full vs restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Full Triangle Congruence Axiom (side-angle-side determines congruence irrespective of orientation) vs restricted version (requires triangles to have same orientation in the plane before applying SAS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full axiom licenses 'flipping' (orientation-reversing congruence); restricted axiom disallows flipping. Hilbert asks whether the broader axiom contains a superfluous part (i.e., whether full SAS is a logical consequence of the restricted version). He shows restricted + ITT implies full (with extra assumptions), but independence results demonstrate subtle interactions with continuity axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom der Nachbarschaft (Axiom of Neighbourhood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any segment AB, there exists a triangle (or square etc.) in whose interior there is no segment congruent to AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert shows that restricted congruence + Archimedean Axiom + Nachbarschaft suffices to prove ITT in one approach. Nachbarschaft is a continuity-style axiom Hilbert used to recover ITT without the unrestricted congruence axiom. Later variants/simplifications (Bernays) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom der Einlagerung (Axiom of Embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one polygon is embedded in another (its boundary contains interior but no exterior points of the first), then it is not possible to split the two polygons into the same number of pairwise congruent triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert introduces Einlagerung as an alternative continuity/intuition-style axiom to Nachbarschaft which, together with other axioms, can help secure ITT; Bernays provided simplifications; Schmidt’s later editions revise the use of these axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean Axiom (continuity assumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasi-numerical continuity axiom (the usual Archimedean property) whose adoption can make ITT provable from restricted congruence axioms; without it, ITT can fail in constructed geometries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert shows that the ITT and the broad congruence axiom become provable when continuity assumptions like the Archimedean Axiom are added. The axiom is quasi-numerical and its inclusion represents a choice between spatial assumptions (like allowing flipping) and continuity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-Archimedean field models to show independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of analytic geometries over non-Archimedean fields (power series field T) to produce models where plane axioms and Nachbarschaft hold but Archimedean Axiom and ITT fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s model uses elements represented by power series in t, with ordering by leading coefficient, producing infinitesimals. Defines points as pairs in T, lines by linear equations, and specially defined rotation maps to satisfy congruence axioms while violating Archimedean consequences; shows concrete independence results and illuminates hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of congruence via parallel transport and rotation mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments are congruent if, after parallel transport to the origin, one can be rotated into the other by a positive rotation through some angle θ; rotation is implemented by an exponential-like map in the complex extension of T: x' + iy' = e^{iθ+(1+i)τ}·(x + iy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s rotation mapping over the non-Archimedean field is the technical device that makes the congruence axioms hold in his model. Important consequences: rotation can change 'length' (rotation sometimes does), so the notion of length depends on the chosen transformation function; verifying the congruence axioms requires careful checking of these mappings (Schmidt provides detailed verifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean Triangle Property
rubrics_metrics.description: The property that the sum of two sides of a triangle is always greater than the third (used as a logical/mathematical benchmark in Hilbert’s investigations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert connects this property to the restricted congruence axiom and to continuity assumptions. In his non-Archimedean model OB + BA' < OA' shows failure of this Euclidean triangle property, illustrating that classical triangle inequalities can fail without appropriate axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of triangle area / Flächenmaß dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert’s reconstruction of triangle area theory (defining area as half base times height) requires that this quantity be independent of which side is chosen as base; this independence depends on similarity/congruence arguments that may require the unrestricted Triangle Congruence Axiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing base-independence requires recognizing similarity of certain right triangles; those triangles are not in the same orientation, so restricted congruence may be insufficient. Therefore the full congruence axiom can be essential for establishing the usual theory of area without extra continuity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Chord Theorem (TCT) and hidden existence assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem that the three chords generated by three mutually intersecting circles in a plane always meet at a common point; Hilbert’s direct proof assumes the circles are equators of spheres intersecting in exactly two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s proof reveals a hidden existence assumption (that three spheres intersect in two points). Purity-of-method scrutiny asks which axioms guarantee the required existence facts; this ties the TCT to triangle-inequality and line-circle/circle-circle properties and so to continuity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-circle property
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line has both a point in the interior of a circle and a point outside it, then it must intersect the circle, and in exactly two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property underlies the definition of power of a point and is implicitly used in Euclid’s constructions; Hilbert shows it need not follow from Axiom Groups I–III alone. Its failure in some models explains failures of geometric constructions like constructing a triangle from three lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle-circle property
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle which has points both inside and outside another circle intersects that other circle in exactly two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is closely related to the line-circle property and is the existential geometric fact implicitly used in Euclid I.1 and I.22. Hilbert’s model constructions demonstrate that circle-circle intersection cannot be taken for granted without suitable continuity/field-completeness assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle Inequality Property (constructability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The property that given three line segments such that any two together are greater than the third, one can construct a triangle with those segments as sides (Euclid I.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert shows that in certain minimal/countable Pythagorean-field based models the requisite points do not exist and thus no triangle can be constructed even though the length inequalities hold; thus constructability depends on stronger field/continuity properties than Axiom Groups I–III provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean vs Euclidean ordered field distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered field is Pythagorean if x^2 + y^2 has a square root in the field whenever x,y are in the field; it is Euclidean if every non-negative element has a square root (i.e., closed under square roots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert uses minimal Pythagorean subfields (e.g., the smallest Pythagorean subfield containing 1 and π) to build models of geometry where certain analytic/geometric points are missing (like sqrt(1-(π/4)^2)), exhibiting failures of circle-circle/line-circle/triangle-constructability properties. This algebraic distinction is a tool for judging which numerical/continuity axioms are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criterion: use of higher mathematics to inform intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should suspend intuitive appeals during logical analysis but ultimately aim to inform and correct geometrical intuition; higher-level logico-mathematical analysis can instruct lower-level geometrical intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes emancipation from intuition during axiomatic analysis, yet regards intuition as the eventual goal or 'Zielpunkt'. Thus methodological evaluation includes whether axiomatic results yield insights that revise or instruct geometric intuition (e.g., using complex analysis over non-Archimedean fields to show elementary geometric failures).
